questions.prompt: How is a virus different from a living cell like a bacterium?
options: It is not a cell - it holds genetic material and needs a host
It is a giant animal cell
It can photosynthesize like a plant
It has a nucleus and many organelles
questions.explanation: A virus is not a cell; it is just a package of genetic material in a coat that must take over a living cell to copy itself.
questions.misconception: The most common mix-up is picturing a virus as a tiny living cell. It is far simpler - no nucleus, no organelles - and it cannot reproduce on its own.

questions.prompt: What is a virus made of?
options: Genetic material (DNA or RNA) wrapped in a protein coat
A shell made of solid stone
questions.explanation: A virus is built of its genetic material (either DNA or RNA) held inside a protein coat, sometimes with spikes on the outside.
questions.misconception: A virus has no organs or watery skin - it is basically trucking its genetic info in a protein coat until it finds a host.

questions.prompt: Why can't a virus reproduce on its own?
options: It has no machinery of its own and must use a host cell
It is too lazy to grow
It can only reproduce in a laboratory
questions.explanation: A virus lacks the machinery to copy itself. It must enter a living host cell and use the cell's machinery to make new viruses.
questions.misconception: The idea that a virus just splits or divides in air is wrong. It has no working parts of its own, so a host cell is required.

questions.prompt: What happens when a virus enters a body cell?
options: The cell's machinery is used to make many new virus copies
The cell quietly reads nothing at all
The virus simply sits still forever
questions.explanation: When a virus invades a host cell, it forces the cell's machinery to build many new virus particles, which then infect more cells.
questions.misconception: A virus doesn't just 'sit' in a cell. It commandeers the cell's own machinery to build copies, which is what makes an infection spread.
